moves.spoken: This is the Jobava London — Bf4 paired with Nc3, a cross between the Veresov and the London, and my main opening.
e6 is already a small inaccuracy, because it opens a square the knight will jump into.
moves.teaches: In the Jobava, an early ...e6 invites the Nb5 leap — watch for it.

moves.spoken: Nb5 — a fried-liver-style leap transposed to the other wing. The point isn't to win the rook with a fork; it's to plant a maddening knight that Black can't easily remove.
moves.teaches: A knight jump like Nb5 is worth it for the lasting outpost, not just the tactic behind it.

moves.spoken: After Na6 the knight on a6 is stuck out of play, and Black can't kick the b5-knight with a pawn — so we calmly develop the other side.
moves.teaches: Provoke a defender to an offside square, then develop while it languishes.

moves.spoken: c3 in true London style, making sure the centre pawn is rock-solid before anything else.
The bishop goes to d3 rather than e2 — both are fine, but d3 is a touch more active.
Careful now: castling immediately would drop a piece to c4, which severs the knight from the bishop's defense.
moves.teaches: Before castling, check the opponent can't fork away the defender of one of your pieces.

moves.spoken: Support the knight with a4 — a pawn, because pawns are the best defenders of a piece.
moves.teaches: Whenever possible, prop up an advanced piece with a pawn rather than another piece.

moves.spoken: And be ready to give the whole thing up: drop the bishop to c2, don't move the knight, and simply let Black take it — the compensation is real.
moves.teaches: In a gambit-flavored position, offer the piece rather than retreat it; activity is the payment.

moves.spoken: The clever b6 pawn sacrifice forces his knight offside to a8, buying us time — his knight now has to trek all the way back into the game.
moves.teaches: Sacrifice a pawn to shove an enemy piece to the corner; the tempi it loses are your compensation.

moves.spoken: While his knight is exiled, we complete development and start piling onto the king, combined with pressure down the a-file.
moves.plans: Finish developing, then attack the king and the a-file together.

moves.spoken: Ne5 centralizes the knight on its best square while his own knight is still marooned on a8.
g4 launches the attack — we have to use this window before Black reroutes his pieces to the queenside.
moves.teaches: When you're ahead in development, strike before the opponent untangles.

moves.spoken: Bring the queen in with Qf3, keep the a-file with Ra1, and prepare e4 to blow the centre open — tighten the noose from every side.
moves.plans: Qf3 and Ra1, then e4 to open lines against the king.
